claim: MCP authorization spec: server acts as OAuth 2.1 resource server, MUST implement RFC9728 protected resource metadata, MUST validate token audience, MUST NOT pass through tokens, clients MUST use RFC8707 resource indicator and PKCE S256.
quote: A protected MCP server acts as an OAuth 2.1 resource server... MCP servers MUST validate that access tokens were issued specifically for them as the intended audience, according to RFC 8707... The MCP server MUST NOT pass through the token it received from the MCP client.

claim: MCP security best practices: confused-deputy via static client ID + dynamic registration + consent cookie; token passthrough explicitly forbidden; session hijacking; local server compromise via startup command; scope minimization.
quote: MCP servers MUST NOT accept any tokens that were not explicitly issued for the MCP server.

claim: Spec evolution: 2025-03-26 used hardcoded /authorize /token /register endpoints; 2025-06-18 separated resource server from authorization server, mandated RFC9728 and RFC8707, prohibited token passthrough.
quote: The June revision also explicitly prohibits MCP servers from passing through tokens to upstream APIs, preventing confused deputy vulnerabilities.

claim: The 2025-11-25 spec formally classifies MCP servers as OAuth 2.1 resource servers and mandates RFC8707 resource indicators to prevent token misuse.
quote: A key feature of the 2025-11-25 specification is the formal classification of MCP servers as OAuth 2.1 resource servers.

claim: Tool poisoning: models see full tool descriptions while users see summaries; hidden instructions in tool metadata trick the agent into exfiltrating SSH keys/files. Shadowing attack: a malicious server poisons descriptions to hijack a trusted server's tools. Mitigations: show full descriptions, pin tool versions by checksum, isolate servers.
quote: a malicious server can hijack an agent without ever appearing explicitly in the agent's user-facing interaction log.

claim: Invariant demonstrated a benign-looking MCP server whose tool description instructs the agent to read the user's WhatsApp history (via a trusted whatsapp-mcp server) and exfiltrate it through ordinary message traffic, evading DLP.
quote: Chat history gets exfiltrated through what looks like ordinary traffic.

claim: Invariant Labs published reproducible code snippets demonstrating MCP tool poisoning and shadowing attacks.
quote: Code snippets to reproduce MCP tool poisoning attacks.

claim: Concrete MCP threats and mitigations: tool poisoning (signature checks, version-lock), prompt injection via tool results (context sanitization), over-permissioned tools (least privilege), supply-chain (registry governance, provenance), rug pull (registry integrity, change monitoring).
quote: Strict input validation and sanitization involves filtering all inputs, from user queries to tool metadata, for dangerous patterns, hidden commands, or suspicious payloads before reaching LLM agents.

claim: CVE-2025-49596 (CVSS 9.4): MCP Inspector before 0.14.1 lacked auth between client and proxy, allowing unauthenticated RCE on developer machines via a malicious website chaining 0.0.0.0-day and CSRF. Fixed in 0.14.1 with session auth and DNS-rebinding/CSRF protection.
quote: By default, the proxy server allows unauthenticated connections and lacks encryption, granting it the power to spawn local processes and execute commands.

claim: Timeline of MCP CVEs/incidents: CVE-2025-6514 (mcp-remote OS command injection RCE on clients via malicious authorization_endpoint), CVE-2025-53109/53110 (Anthropic Filesystem MCP sandbox escape/symlink bypass), Asana cross-tenant data exposure (June 2025), GitHub MCP prompt injection (May 2025).
quote: CVE-2025-6514 – mcp-remote: Critical OS command-injection bug allowing remote code execution on client machines via malicious authorization_endpoint.

claim: Official MCP TypeScript SDK provides StreamableHTTPServerTransport, requireBearerAuth Express middleware, and protected-resource-metadata router for resource-server-mode auth.
quote: The official TypeScript SDK for Model Context Protocol servers and clients

claim: TS SDK production auth pattern: run StreamableHTTPServerTransport behind Express, publish /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource per RFC9728, validate bearer tokens with jose enforcing RFC8707 resource indicators, and check authInfo.scopes inside every tool handler.
quote: publish /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource per RFC 9728, validate bearer tokens with jose while enforcing RFC 8707 resource indicators, and check authInfo.scopes inside every tool handler.

claim: requireBearerAuth is Express middleware that validates the Bearer token via an OAuthTokenVerifier and attaches the resulting AuthInfo to req.auth, surfaced to tool handlers as authInfo.
quote: requireBearerAuth is an Express middleware that requires a valid Bearer token in the Authorization header.

claim: OWASP classifies MCP Tool Poisoning as an indirect prompt-injection attack targeting AI agents connecting to external tool servers via MCP.
quote: MCP Tool Poisoning is an indirect prompt injection attack targeting AI agents that connect to external tool servers via the Model Context Protocol.

claim: CVE-2025-54136 (a.k.a. MCPoison) is a structural tool-poisoning vulnerability where an approved tool definition is silently swapped (rug pull) after the user has trusted it.
quote: MCP Tool Poisoning (CVE-2025-54136): A Structural Vulnerability in Agent Context

claim: Early 2026 saw an unprecedented wave of MCP CVE filings (30 CVEs in 60 days) from Check Point, Invariant Labs, Adversa AI and independent researchers.
MCP authorization mandates OAuth 2.1 with PKCE for all clients (public and confidential) to prevent authorization-code interception.
quote: MCP, OAuth 2.1, PKCE, and the Future of AI Authorization

claim: Docker's analysis confirms the WhatsApp MCP exfiltration relied on a poisoned tool description in a benign-looking trivia/addition server reaching across to a trusted whatsapp-mcp server connected to the same agent.
quote: MCP Horror Stories: The WhatsApp Data Exfiltration Attack
